conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Venturi = fixed/precise FiO₂ (the only one) → use in COPD. Cannula/mask/NRB = variable performance.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Summarise the CPAP vs BiPAP exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: CPAP = Type 1 RF (oxygenation — pulmonary oedema, OSA); BiPAP = Type 2 RF (ventilation — COPD + hypercapnia).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Summarise the BiPAP-in-COPD exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: BiPAP in COPD: use when pH 7.25–7.35. pH <7.25 → consider intubation. pH >7.35 → medical treatment first.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Summarise the PEEP exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: PEEP = prevents alveolar collapse, recruits lung, improves oxygenation. Added by HFNC, CPAP/BiPAP, and mechanical ventilator.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: What should nebulisers be driven with in a COPD exacerbation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Air, not O₂ (avoids worsening hypercapnia).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Summarise the escalation ladder exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: Escalation ladder: O₂ → HFNC → NIV → mechanical ventilation → ECMO. Never skip steps without clinical indication.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.front: Summarise the ECMO exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and.back: ECMO = reversible failure only, specialist centres. Not a long-term solution — a bridge to recovery or transplant.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is respiratory failure, and how is it defined?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: The lungs fail to oxygenate and/or remove CO₂, defined on ABG.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the central fork in respiratory failure, and what does it drive?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Type 1 (oxygenation failure) vs Type 2 (ventilation failure) — drives the cause, management, and which NIV to use.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the ABG definition of Type 1 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: ↓PaO₂ (<8 kPa), normal or low CO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the ABG definition of Type 2 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: ↓PaO₂ + ↑PaCO₂ (>6 kPa).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the core problem in Type 1 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Oxygenation failure (V/Q mismatch — blood not oxygenated).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the core problem in Type 2 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Ventilation failure (can't blow off CO₂).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What are the causes of Type 1 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Pneumonia, PE, pulmonary oedema, ARDS, asthma (early), ILD.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What are the causes of Type 2 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: COPD (commonest), severe asthma (late/tiring), neuromuscular disease (GBS, MND), opiates, obesity hypoventilation / OSA, chest wall deformity.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the commonest cause of Type 2 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: COPD.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Which form of NIV is used in Type 1 respiratory failure, and what does it do?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: CPAP — improves oxygenation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Which form of NIV is used in Type 2 respiratory failure, and what does it do?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: BiPAP — actively ventilates (↓CO₂).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the O₂ target in Type 1 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: 94–98% (standard).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the O₂ target in Type 2 respiratory failure, and why?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: 88–92% (controlled — to avoid worsening hypercapnia).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the tie-in rule linking respiratory failure type to NIV?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Type 1 → CPAP (oxygenation problem); Type 2 → BiPAP (ventilation problem).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the danger sign of a tiring Type 1 respiratory failure patient?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Type 1 RF has ↓PaO₂ with low/normal CO₂ (patient hyperventilating to compensate); as the patient tires → respiratory muscles fail → can no longer hyperventilate → CO₂ starts to rise → normal or rising CO₂ = danger signal → progresses to Type 2 RF → exhaustion → arrest.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Why is a normal or rising CO₂ a danger signal in a Type 1 RF patient?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: It signals the patient is tiring — respiratory muscles can no longer hyperventilate, heralding progression to Type 2 RF, exhaustion, and arrest.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Why is a normal PCO₂ life-threatening in acute asthma?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: The patient should be blowing off CO₂; normalisation = exhaustion.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What are the clinical features of hypoxia (both types of RF)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Dyspnoea, tachypnoea, cyanosis, confusion/agitation, tachycardia, use of accessory muscles.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What are the Type 2-specific (hypercapnia) clinical features?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: CO₂ retention flap (asterixis — outstretched hands), bounding pulse, warm peripheries (vasodilation), headache, drowsiness → coma ('CO₂ narcosis').

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the CO₂ retention flap, and what does it indicate?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Asterixis (a flap on outstretched hands) — a sign of hypercapnia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Why do bounding pulse and warm peripheries occur in Type 2 RF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Vasodilation from ↑CO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: How is Type 1 respiratory failure managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: High-flow O₂ (target 94–98%); CPAP if not responding; treat the cause (e.g. antibiotics for pneumonia, diurese pulmonary oedema); consider HFNC.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: How is Type 2 respiratory failure managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Controlled O₂ (88–92%); BiPAP for respiratory acidosis (pH 7.25–7.35); treat the cause (bronchodilators for COPD, reverse opiates with naloxone); escalate to intubation if pH <7.25.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: At what pH is BiPAP indicated in Type 2 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: pH 7.25–7.35 (respiratory acidosis).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: When should you escalate to intubation in Type 2 respiratory failure?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: If pH <7.25.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Severe Type 1 respiratory failure caused by increased alveolar-capillary permeability → protein-rich fluid floods the alveoli → non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema → atelectasis, ↓compliance, refractory hypoxia. The heart is fine — the capillaries are leaky.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the key distinction of ARDS pulmonary oedema from cardiac causes?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: It is non-cardiogenic — the heart is fine, the capillaries are leaky.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the commonest cause of ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Sepsis / pneumonia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: List the inflammatory insults that cause ARDS.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Sepsis/pneumonia (commonest), aspiration of gastric contents, massive blood transfusion (TRALI), major trauma/burns, acute pancreatitis, COVID-19, cardiopulmonary bypass.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the unifying theme of ARDS aetiology?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: A massive inflammatory insult (pulmonary or systemic) → diffuse alveolar damage → capillary leak → non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What are the clinical features of ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Acute severe dyspnoea, tachypnoea, refractory hypoxia (doesn't correct with O₂), bilateral fine crackles, low SpO₂ despite high FiO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the hallmark of ARDS, and why does it distinguish it from other Type 1 RF?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Refractory hypoxia — hypoxia that does not correct with supplemental oxygen alone (distinguishes ARDS from most other causes of Type 1 RF).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is Berlin Criterion 1 for ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Acute onset — within 1 week of a known clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is Berlin Criterion 2 for ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Bilateral infiltrates — CXR or CT showing bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusion, lobar collapse, or nodules. Resembles pulmonary oedema + air bronchograms.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is Berlin Criterion 3 for ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Non-cardiogenic — respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload. Echo or wedge pressure if doubt.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is Berlin Criterion 4 for ARDS, including the severity grades?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio <300 mmHg (<40 kPa): mild 200–300 mmHg, moderate 100–200 mmHg, severe <100 mmHg. Lower ratio = worse disease.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio defines severe ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: <100 mmHg.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Is there a specific cure for ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: No — management is supportive (no specific cure).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: How is the cause treated in ARDS management?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Antibiotics for sepsis/pneumonia, amylase monitoring for pancreatitis, stop offending transfusion (TRALI). Cause treatment is the only disease-modifying step.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is lung-protective ventilation in ARDS, and why is it used?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Low tidal volume (~6 mL/kg ideal body weight) — avoids volutrauma. Adequate PEEP — prevents repeated alveolar collapse/re-opening. Permissive hypercapnia is acceptable.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What tidal volume is used in lung-protective ventilation for ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Low tidal volume, ~6 mL/kg ideal body weight.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the role of PEEP in ARDS ventilation?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: It prevents repeated alveolar collapse/re-opening.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is permissive hypercapnia in ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Allowing a higher CO₂ is acceptable as part of lung-protective ventilation (low tidal volume).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the role of prone positioning in ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: 12–16 hours/day — promotes uniform lung inflation, ↓dorsal atelectasis, improves V/Q matching. Mortality benefit in moderate-severe ARDS.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: In which ARDS severity does prone positioning give a mortality benefit?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Moderate-severe ARDS.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What supportive / ITU measures are used in ARDS?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Conservative fluid balance (avoid further oedema); vasopressors; renal support; ECMO if refractory. High mortality (30–60%).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: What is the mortality of ARDS?
Summarise the Type 1 vs Type 2 RF exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Type 1 = hypoxia alone (oxygenation failure, normal/low CO₂) → CPAP. Type 2 = hypoxia + ↑CO₂ (ventilation failure) → BiPAP.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Summarise the tiring-Type-1 danger sign exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Tiring Type 1 → rising CO₂ = danger sign (exhaustion). Normal CO₂ in acute asthma is life-threatening.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Summarise the O₂ target exam pearl for Type 1 vs Type 2.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Type 2 O₂ target 88–92%; Type 1 94–98%. Never give high O₂ freely to CO₂ retainers.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Summarise the ARDS exam pearl (mechanism and severity).
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: ARDS = non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema — leaky capillaries, heart is fine. It is a severe Type 1 RF.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Summarise the Berlin criteria exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: Acute (<1 wk) + bilateral infiltrates + non-cardiogenic + PaO₂/FiO₂ <300 mmHg.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.front: Summarise the ARDS management exam pearl.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Fai.back: ARDS Rx: low tidal volume (6 mL/kg) + PEEP + prone positioning; treat cause; ITU. No specific cure.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is VTE composed of, and how are DVT and PE related?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: VTE = DVT + PE — the same disease, two ends. Clot forms in the deep veins (usually legs) → embolises to the pulmonary arteries.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the significance of PE in maternal and post-operative mortality?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: VTE/PE is the leading cause of DIRECT maternal death (cardiac disease is the leading cause overall, per MBRRACE-UK), and is a major cause of post-operative mortality — hence universal VTE risk assessment and thromboprophylaxis.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the two diagnostic spines and the management fork for PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Diagnostic spines: Wells score → D-dimer/CTPA. Management fork: stable → anticoagulate / unstable → thrombolyse.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: Outline the pathophysiology of PE from thrombus to arrest.
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Thrombus obstructs the pulmonary artery → V/Q mismatch (ventilated but not perfused) → ↑pulmonary vascular resistance → acute right heart strain → massive PE: RV failure → obstructive shock → arrest.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the V/Q mismatch in PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: The lung is ventilated but not perfused.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the three components of Virchow's triad?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the causes of stasis in Virchow's triad?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Immobility, long-haul flights, surgery, heart failure, paralysis, pregnancy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the causes of endothelial injury in Virchow's triad?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Trauma, surgery, smoking, vasculitis, central lines.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the causes of hypercoagulability in Virchow's triad?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Cancer (especially mucin-secreting), pregnancy, OCP/HRT, Factor V Leiden, thrombophilia, antiphospholipid syndrome, SLE, polycythaemia.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the non-thrombotic causes of emboli?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Fat (long-bone fracture), air (central line, scuba), amniotic fluid (obstetric emergency), tumour.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What VTE prophylaxis is given to all admissions?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: VTE risk-assess on admission; LMWH (enoxaparin) — pharmacological; compression stockings / TED stockings — mechanical; early mobilisation.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the contraindications to LMWH prophylaxis?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Active bleeding, thrombocytopenia, acute stroke (haemorrhagic).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the contraindications to compression/TED stockings?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: PAD (peripheral arterial disease), severe leg oedema, neuropathy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the clinical features of a small/medium PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, haemoptysis, tachycardia, tachypnoea, low-grade fever, pleural rub.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the clinical features of a massive PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Central chest pain, shock/collapse, cyanosis, ↑JVP, RV heave, loud P2 or gallop rhythm — signs of acute right heart strain.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the signs of a DVT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Unilateral leg — swelling, warmth, tenderness, erythema. Calf circumference >3cm difference = significant.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What calf circumference difference is considered significant in DVT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: >3cm difference.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the classic PE vignette?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Post-op / long-haul flight patient + sudden SOB + pleuritic chest pain + tachycardia ± leg swelling.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the key components of the Wells 2-level PE score?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Clinical DVT signs (+3), PE most likely diagnosis (+3), heart rate >100 (+1.5), immobilisation/surgery <4wks (+1.5), prior DVT/PE (+1.5), haemoptysis (+1), active malignancy (+1).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: How is a Wells score >4 (PE likely) managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Immediate CTPA. Start interim anticoagulation if any delay. CTPA +ve → treat; CTPA −ve → consider leg USS.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: How is a Wells score ≤4 (PE unlikely) managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: D-dimer first. D-dimer −ve → stop, consider alternative diagnosis. D-dimer +ve → CTPA.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: How is a haemodynamically unstable patient too sick for CTPA managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Bedside echo (RV dilatation = strong presumptive evidence) → thrombolyse empirically. Do not delay for imaging.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: CTPA — confirms PE, delineates extent, most sensitive/specific.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: When is a V/Q scan used in PE, and how is it reported?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: If CTPA is contraindicated: renal impairment, contrast allergy, pregnancy. Reports as high/intermediate/low probability.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: How is D-dimer used in PE, and what are its limitations?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: High sensitivity, poor specificity. Use to rule OUT in low-probability only. Raised in cancer, pregnancy, post-op, infection, age. Never used to rule in.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the commonest ECG finding in PE, and what is the classic but rare one?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Usually sinus tachycardia (commonest). RV strain: T inversion V1–4, RBBB, RAD. Classic but rare: S1Q3T3.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What does the ABG show in PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Hypoxaemia + hypocapnia → respiratory alkalosis (blowing off CO₂ due to hyperventilation).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What does the CXR usually show in PE, and what are the rare findings?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Usually normal. Rarely: wedge infarct, Westermark's sign (oligaemia distal to clot), raised hemidiaphragm, effusion.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is Westermark's sign?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Oligaemia distal to the clot on CXR.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the role of echo in PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Bedside for unstable patients — RV dilatation/strain; rules out other causes (tamponade, LV failure).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: When is a confirmed proximal DVT on leg USS sufficient to treat as VTE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Proximal DVT confirmed → sufficient to treat as VTE even without CTPA.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What blood tests are used in PE and what do they reflect?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: FBC, U&Es, LFTs, coagulation, troponin (RV stress), BNP (severity); thrombophilia screen after treatment.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the first-line management of a haemodynamically stable PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: DOAC first-line: apixaban or rivaroxaban — start immediately (no heparin lead-in needed); dabigatran or edoxaban — need 5 days LMWH lead-in first.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: Which DOACs need a 5-day LMWH lead-in, and which can start immediately?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Apixaban or rivaroxaban start immediately (no lead-in); dabigatran or edoxaban need a 5-day LMWH lead-in first.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: Which exceptions to DOAC use in stable PE require LMWH bridge to warfarin?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Renal failure / antiphospholipid syndrome (triple positive) → LMWH bridge → warfarin (INR 2–3).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: Why must warfarin be bridged with heparin until the INR is therapeutic?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Warfarin is initially prothrombotic (↓Proteins C & S first), so must bridge with heparin until the INR is therapeutic.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the key intervention for a haemodynamically unstable (massive) PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Thrombolysis (alteplase) — the key intervention. Supportive: O₂, cautious IV fluids (RV is preload-sensitive), ICU, vasopressors.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: Why must IV fluids be cautious in a massive PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Because the RV is preload-sensitive.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the options if thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails in massive PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Surgical embolectomy or IVC filter; percutaneous catheter-directed therapy is an option in specialist centres.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the duration of anticoagulation for a provoked PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: 3 months (clear precipitant, e.g. surgery, fracture).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the duration of anticoagulation for an unprovoked PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: ≥3–6 months; reassess; many need indefinite (no identifiable cause).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the duration of anticoagulation for PE with active cancer / antiphospholipid / thrombophilia?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Indefinite (ongoing risk).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the clinical features of a DVT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Unilateral leg — swelling, warmth, erythema, tenderness along the vein. Calf circumference >3cm difference = significant. May have Homan's sign (unreliable — calf pain on dorsiflexion).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is Homan's sign, and how reliable is it?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Calf pain on dorsiflexion — unreliable.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: How is a DVT diagnosed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: 2-level DVT Wells score → if likely: proximal leg USS (compression USS). If unlikely: D-dimer → USS if positive. Proximal DVT confirmed = treat as VTE.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: How is a DVT managed?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Same as PE — DOAC first-line (apixaban/rivaroxaban); duration by provoked/unprovoked. Compression stockings for post-thrombotic prevention.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What are the complications of a DVT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: PE (embolisation — commonest serious complication); post-thrombotic syndrome (chronic venous insufficiency → leg pain, swelling, skin changes, ulcers).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the commonest serious complication of a DVT?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: PE (embolisation).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is post-thrombotic syndrome?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Chronic venous insufficiency → leg pain, swelling, skin changes, ulcers.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: Why should DOACs not be used in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Higher failure rate — use LMWH → warfarin (INR 2–3) instead.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the PERC rule?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: PE Rule-Out Criteria — if ALL 8 criteria met in low-risk patient: no D-dimer needed (PE excluded). Criteria: age <50, HR <100, SpO₂ ≥95%, no leg swelling/DVT, no haemoptysis, no oestrogen use, no prior PE/DVT, no surgery/trauma in 4 weeks.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the PESI score?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index — predicts 30-day mortality: class I/II = low risk (consider home treatment); class III–V = higher risk (admit). Variables: age, cancer, HR, BP, respiratory rate, temperature, mental status, SpO₂.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is the difference between submassive and massive PE?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Massive PE: haemodynamic instability (SBP <90 mmHg or drop >40 mmHg) — emergency thrombolysis. Submassive: haemodynamically stable but RV dysfunction. Low-risk: no RV strain.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is Hampton's hump?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Peripheral wedge-shaped opacity on CXR representing pulmonary infarction — points towards the hilum. Specific for PE but uncommon (~5%).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is pulmonary infarction?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Tissue death from PE — occurs peripherally (the dual bronchial-artery supply usually protects central lung). Presents with pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis and fever. CXR may show a wedge-shaped peripheral opacity (Hampton's hump), often with a small pleural effusion.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Late complication of PE — unresolved thrombus organises and obstructs pulmonary vasculature → progressive pulmonary hypertension, RV failure, dyspnoea. Treated by pulmonary endarterectomy.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is McConnell's sign?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: Echo finding in acute PE: RV free wall hypokinesis with sparing of the RV apex — relatively specific for acute pulmonary embolism (vs chronic RV failure).

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: When can PE be treated at home (outpatient)?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: PESI class I/II (low risk) + no haemodynamic instability + adequate home support + DOAC suitable — NICE supports early discharge or outpatient treatment for low-risk PE.

conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.front: What is massive PE mortality without treatment?
conditions__RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embol.back: ~30–35% mortality without treatment. With appropriate anticoagulation: reduced to ~5%. Massive PE with shock: mortality >50% without immediate intervention.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What epithelium lines most of the conducting (upper) airway, and what is its full descriptive name?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Respiratory epithelium = pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells (PCCE).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What are the two main functions of respiratory epithelium?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Conditioning inspired air (warming, humidifying, filtering) and mucociliary clearance of trapped debris and microbes.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: List regions lined by respiratory (PCCE) epithelium.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Most of the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, nasopharynx, larynx below the vocal cords, trachea and bronchi.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Why is respiratory epithelium described as 'pseudostratified'?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Every cell contacts the basement membrane, but the nuclei lie at different levels, giving a false appearance of multiple layers.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Which airway epithelial neurons regenerate, and what antibody protects the mucosa?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Olfactory receptor neurons are bipolar neurons continuously replaced from basal stem cells — a rare regenerating neuron. Secretory (dimeric) IgA, transported across the epithelium via the poly-Ig receptor, is the principal mucosal antibody in airway mucus.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Name the five cell types of respiratory epithelium.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Ciliated columnar (most numerous), goblet, basal (stem), brush, and small-granule (neuroendocrine/Kulchitsky) cells.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Which cell of respiratory epithelium is the most numerous and what does it do?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: The ciliated columnar cell; its cilia drive the mucociliary escalator toward the pharynx.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What does the goblet cell secrete and how does it stain?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Mucins forming the gel layer of the mucus blanket; it is PAS-positive and Alcian-blue positive.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What is the role of the basal cell, and why does it make the epithelium look stratified?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: It is the stem/reserve cell that regenerates the other cell types; being short and sitting on the basement membrane, its low nucleus adds to the layered appearance.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What is a brush cell?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: A columnar cell bearing blunt microvilli that acts as a chemosensory receptor, with an afferent nerve ending at its base.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What is the small-granule (neuroendocrine/Kulchitsky) cell and its clinical importance?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: A DNES cell with dense-core granules (serotonin, bombesin); it is the cell of origin of bronchial carcinoid and small-cell carcinoma.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Describe the two layers of the airway mucus blanket.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: A watery sol (periciliary) layer in which the cilia beat, and an overlying sticky gel layer that traps particles and microbes.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Describe the ciliary beat cycle.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: A fast forward power stroke whose tip engages the gel layer to push mucus toward the pharynx, followed by a slow recovery stroke within the sol layer.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What is the ultrastructure of a motile cilium?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: A '9 + 2' axoneme — nine peripheral microtubule doublets plus a central pair — with dynein arms that use ATP to slide the doublets, anchored by a basal body.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Which epithelium lines the nasal vestibule?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Stratified squamous keratinised epithelium, with vibrissae (hairs) and sebaceous glands.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Which epithelium covers the true vocal cords and why?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Stratified squamous (non-keratinised) epithelium, to withstand the abrasion of vibration.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Where is olfactory epithelium located and what special cells does it contain?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: In the roof of the nasal cavity; it contains olfactory receptor neurons, sustentacular (supporting) cells and basal cells, with Bowman's glands beneath.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: How does the epithelium change across the epiglottis?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Stratified squamous on the lingual/upper surface transitions to respiratory epithelium on the lower (laryngeal) surface.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: How does the nose warm inspired air?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Rich venous plexuses/swell bodies in the nasal conchae radiate heat to the air (and cause the alternating nasal cycle).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Contrast the epithelium of the true vocal cords, false cords and adenoid.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: True vocal cords: stratified squamous (to withstand vibration). False (vestibular) cords: respiratory pseudostratified ciliated columnar. The adenoid (pharyngeal tonsil) is also covered by respiratory PCCE, unlike the squamous-covered palatine and lingual tonsils.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What is Waldeyer's ring?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: The ring of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (pharyngeal, palatine, tubal and lingual tonsils) guarding the entrance to the aerodigestive tract.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Which stains highlight goblet-cell and gland mucin?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: PAS (magenta) and Alcian blue (blue).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What is squamous metaplasia of the respiratory tract and its main cause?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Replacement of ciliated/goblet respiratory epithelium by stratified squamous epithelium, classically caused by cigarette smoking; it loses mucociliary clearance and can progress to dysplasia and squamous cell carcinoma.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What is primary ciliary dyskinesia and the features of Kartagener syndrome?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: An autosomal recessive dynein-arm defect causing dysmotile cilia; the Kartagener triad is situs inversus, chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis (with male infertility as a further PCD feature). Screen with low nasal nitric oxide.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What are the histological features of allergic rhinitis?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Type I hypersensitivity change with mucosal oedema, eosinophil infiltrate and goblet-cell/gland hypersecretion.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: What are nasal polyps and what conditions are they associated with?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: Oedematous, inflamed protrusions of respiratory mucosa; associated with chronic rhinosinusitis, aspirin sensitivity and cystic fibrosis.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Where is Little's area and why is it clinically important?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: On the anterior nasal septum (Kiesselbach's plexus); it is the commonest site of epistaxis (nosebleeds).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.front: Contrast the mucus defect in cystic fibrosis and primary ciliary dyskinesia.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Upper Respirator.back: In CF, defective CFTR chloride/water secretion dehydrates the periciliary layer, so normal cilia beat in thick sticky mucus. In PCD, the mucus is normal but the cilia are structurally abnormal (dynein-arm defect) and cannot beat. Both stall the mucociliary escalator, causing sinusitis and bronchiectasis.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: List the airway generations from trachea to the start of gas exchange.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Trachea -> main (primary) bronchi -> lobar -> segmental bronchi -> bronchioles -> terminal bronchioles -> respiratory bronchioles (where gas exchange begins).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What are the four structural trends as you move distally down the airway tree?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Epithelium becomes shorter (columnar -> cuboidal), cartilage and glands disappear, goblet cells disappear, and smooth muscle becomes relatively more prominent.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What is the single best histological feature distinguishing a bronchus from a bronchiole?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Bronchi have cartilage plates and submucosal glands; bronchioles have neither.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Describe the epithelium and key wall features of a bronchus.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells; a continuous spiral smooth-muscle band; submucosal seromucous glands; irregular hyaline cartilage plates; and a fibroelastic adventitia.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: How does the cartilage change from trachea to intrapulmonary bronchus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: The C-shaped tracheal rings break up into irregular plates/islands that encircle the intrapulmonary bronchus, and a complete smooth-muscle layer appears.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Define a bronchiole and give its size and key negatives.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: An airway <=1 mm in diameter with no cartilage, no glands and (in the terminal bronchiole) no goblet cells; it has a relatively prominent smooth-muscle layer.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What epithelium lines bronchioles?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Simple ciliated columnar proximally, becoming simple cuboidal (often still ciliated) distally, with club cells.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What holds bronchioles open, given they lack cartilage?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Radial traction from the elastic recoil of the surrounding alveolar walls, plus smooth-muscle tone.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Why are bronchioles the critical site of obstruction in asthma and COPD?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: They have no cartilage to splint them open, so smooth-muscle contraction and loss of elastic traction readily narrow or collapse them.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What is the terminal bronchiole and what does it supply?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: The last purely conducting airway; each terminal bronchiole supplies one pulmonary acinus. (A secondary pulmonary lobule — the HRCT unit bounded by connective-tissue septa — is fed by several, ~3–5, terminal bronchioles.)

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What are club (Clara) cells and where are they found?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Dome-shaped, non-ciliated secretory cells of the bronchiolar epithelium that increase distally.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: List the functions of club cells.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Secrete surfactant-like material and club-cell secretory protein (CC16) to reduce surface tension and protect the lining; detoxify inhaled xenobiotics via cytochrome P450; and act as progenitor/stem cells for the bronchiolar epithelium.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What are neuroepithelial bodies?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Innervated clusters of pulmonary neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells at bronchiolar bifurcations that act as hypoxia chemoreceptors, releasing serotonin and bombesin; they are the cell of origin of bronchial carcinoid and small-cell carcinoma.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What defines a respiratory bronchiole?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: A bronchiole whose cuboidal wall is interrupted by scattered alveoli — the first airway where gas exchange occurs.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What is the pulmonary acinus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Everything distal to a single terminal bronchiole — the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli — i.e. the functional gas-exchange unit.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Where is the boundary between the conducting and respiratory zones?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: The terminal bronchiole ends the conducting zone; the respiratory bronchiole begins the respiratory (gas-exchange) zone.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What is the Reid index and when is it increased?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: The ratio of submucosal gland thickness to total bronchial wall thickness; it is increased (>0.4) in chronic bronchitis due to gland hypertrophy.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What are the histological features of asthma in the airways?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Bronchiolar smooth-muscle hyperplasia and hypertrophy, bronchoconstriction, mucus plugging, subepithelial basement-membrane fibrosis, goblet-cell metaplasia and eosinophilic inflammation; sputum shows Curschmann spirals and Charcot-Leyden crystals. The airflow obstruction is reversible.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What is chronic bronchitis histologically?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Submucosal gland hypertrophy (increased Reid index) and goblet-cell hyperplasia with mucus hypersecretion, producing a chronic productive cough.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What is bronchiectasis?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Permanent, abnormal dilatation of bronchi from chronic infection/obstruction with destruction of the muscle and cartilage of the wall.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: From which cells do bronchial carcinoid and small-cell carcinoma arise?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Bronchial neuroendocrine (small-granule/Kulchitsky) cells.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Why does the lumen of a bronchiole often look folded (scalloped) on a slide?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Contraction of its prominent smooth-muscle layer throws the mucosa into folds.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Distinguish the pulmonary acinus, secondary lobule and primary lobule.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Acinus = everything distal to one terminal bronchiole (the gas-exchange unit). Secondary pulmonary lobule = the polyhedral, septum-bounded unit seen on HRCT, supplied by ~3–5 terminal bronchioles (several acini). Primary lobule = tissue distal to one respiratory bronchiole.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What is Reisseissen's muscle?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: The smooth muscle of the bronchioles, relatively prominent because there is no cartilage; it regulates airway calibre.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Which airway component maintains bronchial patency?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: The hyaline cartilage plates in the bronchial wall.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What lung disease results from loss of radial traction on small airways?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Emphysema/COPD — destruction of alveolar attachments removes the tethering that holds bronchioles open, causing expiratory collapse and airflow limitation.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: What causes bronchiolitis in infants, and what is the lesion?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: Commonly respiratory syncytial virus (RSV); inflammation of the bronchioles with epithelial damage, oedema and mucus that obstruct the small airways.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.front: Trace where the smooth muscle is located relative to the cartilage in a bronchus.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronch.back: The smooth muscle forms a band internal to (deep to) the cartilage plates, between the mucosa/submucosa and the cartilage.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What are alveoli and roughly how many/what surface area do they provide?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: The thin-walled air sacs where gas exchange occurs — about 300 million, giving a total surface area of ~70 m2.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: Off which structures do alveoli open?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: State Fick's law of diffusion in the context of the alveolus.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Diffusion rate is proportional to (surface area x pressure difference) divided by barrier thickness — so the alveolus maximises area and minimises thickness.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What is the interalveolar septum?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: The shared wall between adjacent alveoli, containing the capillary network, pneumocytes, fused basement membranes, elastic/collagen interstitium and macrophages.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: On H&E, how do you usually identify type I pneumocytes?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Mainly by their flat nuclei bulging into the airspace — their gas-exchange cytoplasm is too thin to resolve by light microscopy.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: How do type II pneumocytes appear on a slide?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: As rounded, cuboidal cells at the corners of alveolar septa, with foamy/vacuolated cytoplasm.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: List the three layers of the blood-air barrier that gas crosses.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: (1) Type I pneumocyte cytoplasm plus its surfactant film, (2) the fused basal laminae of the pneumocyte and endothelium, and (3) the capillary endothelial cytoplasm — then plasma and the red-cell membrane to haemoglobin (total ~0.2–0.5 μm).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: How thick is the blood-air barrier?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: About 0.2-0.5 micrometres on the thin (exchange) side.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What is the difference between the thin and thick sides of the septum?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: The thin side has fused pneumocyte and endothelial basement membranes for efficient gas exchange; the thick side contains interstitium (elastic, collagen, fibroblasts, fluid) for support and fluid handling.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: Compare type I and type II pneumocytes in surface area and cell number.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Type I cover ~95% of surface but are ~40% of cell number; type II cover ~5% of surface but are ~60% of cell number (more numerous).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: Which pneumocyte is the gas-exchange cell and can it divide?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: The type I pneumocyte; it is a simple squamous cell that cannot divide (it is replaced by proliferating type II cells).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: Which pneumocyte acts as the stem cell of the alveolus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: The type II pneumocyte, which can regenerate both type I and type II cells.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What is surfactant made of and by which cell?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: A phospholipid-protein film — chiefly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) with phosphatidylglycerol and cholesterol, plus surfactant proteins A-D — made by type II pneumocytes and stored in lamellar bodies.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What is the main function of surfactant?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: It lowers surface tension at the air-liquid interface, preventing alveolar collapse (atelectasis) at end-expiration and reducing the work of breathing.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: How does surfactant relate to Laplace's law?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Laplace's law (P = 2T/r) predicts small alveoli would empty into larger ones; surfactant lowers surface tension more in small alveoli, stabilising them so they stay open.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: When does surfactant production begin and become adequate in the fetus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: It appears around 24 weeks and is usually adequate by about 35 weeks of gestation.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What are the roles of surfactant proteins A/D versus B/C?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: A and D are innate-immune opsonins (collectins); B and C help spread and stabilise the phospholipid film.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What is an alveolar macrophage (dust cell) and where does it come from?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: A tissue-resident phagocyte — chiefly fetal-derived and locally self-renewing (blood monocytes are recruited only during inflammation) — that patrols the airspace and interstitium, ingesting dust, microbes and spent surfactant; it clears via the mucociliary escalator or lymphatics.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What are heart-failure cells?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Haemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages seen in chronic pulmonary venous congestion (e.g. left heart failure); they stain with Perls' Prussian blue.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What are the pores of Kohn and their significance?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Small openings between adjacent alveoli that allow collateral airflow — but also let macrophages, fluid and infection spread from alveolus to alveolus.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: How is fetal lung maturity assessed before delivery?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: By the amniotic-fluid lecithin:sphingomyelin (L:S) ratio — >2 indicates mature surfactant (<2 predicts RDS) — and by the appearance of phosphatidylglycerol; antenatal corticosteroids accelerate maturity while maternal diabetes (fetal hyperinsulinaemia) delays it.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: Which immunomarker identifies type II pneumocytes and lung adenocarcinoma?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: TTF-1 (thyroid transcription factor-1) marks type II pneumocytes and primary lung adenocarcinoma; it is also positive in thyroid tissue/carcinoma, and is used to distinguish a lung primary from a metastasis.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome and its histology?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Surfactant deficiency due to prematurity (worse with maternal diabetes) causing widespread atelectasis and hyaline membranes; prevented by giving the mother antenatal corticosteroids before preterm delivery, and treated with exogenous surfactant plus respiratory support (CPAP/ventilation).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What is a hyaline membrane and in which conditions is it seen?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: A glassy eosinophilic layer of dead cells and plasma proteins lining alveoli, seen in diffuse alveolar damage — ARDS and neonatal RDS.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: How does ARDS damage the alveolus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Diffuse alveolar damage kills type I pneumocytes and leaks protein-rich exudate that forms hyaline membranes; the refractory hypoxaemia is due chiefly to intrapulmonary shunt and V/Q mismatch (flooded, non-ventilated alveoli), which is why it responds to PEEP rather than to supplemental oxygen alone.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: How does emphysema impair gas exchange?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Destruction of alveolar septa reduces the total surface area and elastic recoil available for exchange.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: Why do pulmonary oedema and pulmonary fibrosis both cause hypoxaemia?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Both thicken the blood-air barrier — oedema adds interstitial/alveolar fluid, fibrosis adds collagen — increasing the diffusion distance (Fick's law).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.front: What structural elements give the alveolar septum its elastic recoil?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-.back: Elastic (and collagen) fibres in the interstitium of the septum, produced by fibroblasts.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Which two epithelial cells line the alveolus, and what seals them into a continuous sheet?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Type I and type II pneumocytes, sealed together by tight (occluding) junctions that keep fluid out of the airspace.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Summarise the division of labour between type I and type II pneumocytes.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Type I is the thin squamous gas-exchange surface; type II makes surfactant, clears fluid, provides defence and acts as the alveolar stem cell for repair.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: On light microscopy, why do you usually see only the nucleus of a type I pneumocyte?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Its gas-exchange cytoplasm is only ~0.1-0.2 micrometres thick — below the resolution of the light microscope — so only the flattened nucleus is visible.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Give the surface-area and cell-number percentages for type I pneumocytes.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Type I cells cover ~95% of the alveolar surface but make up only ~40% of the cell number.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Give the surface-area and cell-number percentages for type II pneumocytes.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Type II cells cover ~5% of the surface but make up ~60% of the cell number (they are the more numerous cell).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Why can't type I pneumocytes regenerate the alveolar lining themselves?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: They are terminally differentiated and cannot divide; they are replaced by type II cells that proliferate and transdifferentiate into type I.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Which junction type joins pneumocytes and what does it achieve?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Occluding tight junctions, which form a barrier keeping fluid and solutes out of the alveolar airspace (keeping the alveolus dry).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Name markers of the type I pneumocyte.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Aquaporin-5 (AQP5), podoplanin (T1alpha) and caveolin-1.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Describe the ultrastructure of a type II pneumocyte.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: A cuboidal cell with short apical microvilli, abundant RER and Golgi, and characteristic membrane-bound osmiophilic lamellar bodies storing surfactant.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: What is the diagnostic organelle of the type II pneumocyte?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: The lamellar body — a whorled, osmiophilic, membrane-bound store of surfactant.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: List the four functions of type II pneumocytes.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: (1) Synthesise/secrete/recycle surfactant, (2) act as the alveolar stem/progenitor cell (self-renew and become type I), (3) help clear alveolar fluid via ENaC and Na/K-ATPase, and (4) innate defence (secrete SP-A/SP-D). (Xenobiotic P450 detoxification is mainly the club cell's role.)

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: How do type II pneumocytes keep the alveolus dry?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: They actively pump Na+ (via apical ENaC and basolateral Na/K-ATPase), drawing fluid out of the airspace across the epithelium.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Name markers of the type II pneumocyte.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Surfactant proteins SP-B and SP-C are lineage markers; the diagnostic immunohistochemistry markers used clinically are TTF-1 and Napsin A (Napsin A is an aspartic protease).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Outline the surfactant life-cycle.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Lipids and surfactant proteins are made in RER, processed in Golgi, packaged into lamellar bodies, secreted by exocytosis, unfold into tubular myelin (SP-B and Ca2+ dependent) to feed the surface film, then are recycled by type II cells or cleared by macrophages.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: What is the main lipid of surfactant and roughly what fraction is lipid vs protein?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) is the main lipid; surfactant is ~90% lipid and ~10% protein.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Contrast the roles of surfactant proteins A/D versus B/C.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: SP-A and SP-D are hydrophilic collectins that mediate innate immunity (opsonisation) and, for SP-A, regulate secretion and tubular myelin; SP-B and SP-C are hydrophobic proteins that spread and stabilise the lipid film.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: What is tubular myelin and which surfactant protein is essential for it?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: A lattice-like intermediate form of secreted surfactant that feeds the surface film; it requires SP-A and SP-B (plus calcium) to form.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Why is SP-B deficiency clinically important?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Congenital SP-B deficiency prevents tubular myelin/functional surfactant formation and is lethal in neonates (fatal respiratory failure).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: How is the alveolar lining repaired after type I cell death?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Type II pneumocytes proliferate and then transdifferentiate into new type I cells, restoring the thin gas-exchange surface.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: What histological change signals acute alveolar injury?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Type II (pneumocyte) hyperplasia — a plump cuboidal lining replacing the normal flat type I lining.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Why can reactive type II hyperplasia be a diagnostic pitfall?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: The enlarged, atypical-looking reparative type II cells can mimic malignancy on cytology after ARDS or infection.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: How does aberrant alveolar repair contribute to fibrosis?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Repeated or dysregulated type II-driven repair recruits fibroblasts and deposits collagen instead of cleanly re-epithelialising, producing fibrosis (e.g. IPF).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: What is the histology and cause of neonatal RDS in pneumocyte terms?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Immature type II cells produce insufficient surfactant, causing atelectasis and hyaline membranes; congenital SP-B deficiency is a fatal form.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: What happens to pneumocytes in ARDS / diffuse alveolar damage?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Type I pneumocytes undergo necrosis and hyaline membranes form (exudative phase); reactive type II hyperplasia appears in the organising phase.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Which markers identify lung adenocarcinoma, and which pneumocyte lineage does it reflect?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: TTF-1 and Napsin A; these reflect a type II pneumocyte (or club-cell) lineage. TTF-1 is negative in squamous cell carcinoma (which is p40/p63 positive) but positive in small-cell carcinoma and thyroid, so Napsin A helps confirm adenocarcinoma.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: What is pulmonary alveolar proteinosis?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Accumulation of PAS-positive surfactant material in the alveoli due to defective macrophage clearance, usually from anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: How does high-concentration oxygen damage the alveolus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: It generates free radicals that injure the fragile type I pneumocytes, producing diffuse alveolar damage (a cause of ARDS).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.front: Name the genetic causes of fatal neonatal surfactant deficiency.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneu.back: Congenital SP-B (SFTPB) deficiency and ABCA3 transporter deficiency — both autosomal recessive and lethal in neonates; ABCA3 loads phospholipid into the lamellar bodies. (SP-C/SFTPC mutations instead cause autosomal-dominant familial pulmonary fibrosis in later life.)

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What is the partnership underlying mucociliary clearance?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Goblet cells secrete the sticky mucus that traps particles and microbes, and cilia move that mucus toward the pharynx — together forming the mucociliary escalator, the airway's primary innate defence.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: How does a goblet cell appear on H&E and how does it stain specially?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: A pale, clear, cup-shaped ('goblet') cell with an apical theca of mucin and a nucleus squashed to the base; it is PAS-magenta and Alcian-blue positive.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Describe the ultrastructure of a goblet cell.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: A unicellular exocrine gland with a narrow base containing the nucleus and abundant RER/Golgi, widening into an apical theca packed with mucinogen granules.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Which mucins do goblet cells and submucosal glands secrete?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Goblet cells secrete mainly MUC5AC; submucosal glands add MUC5B — both gel-forming mucins.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: By what mechanism do goblet cells release mucin?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Merocrine exocytosis (regulated release of granule contents without loss of cytoplasm or membrane).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What happens to mucins on hydration?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: They are huge glycoproteins that swell 100-1000 times in water to form the sticky gel layer of the mucus blanket.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: How does goblet-cell number change along the airway?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Goblet cells are numerous in the trachea and bronchi and disappear by the bronchioles, where club (Clara) cells take over the secretory role.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Besides mucins, what antimicrobial substances are in the airway mucus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Lysozyme, lactoferrin, defensins and secretory IgA.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Describe the '9+2' axoneme of a motile cilium.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Nine peripheral microtubule doublets (an A tubule plus an incomplete B tubule) arranged around a central pair of single microtubules.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What are dynein arms and what do they do?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: ATPase motor proteins projecting from the A tubule of each doublet; they generate the force for ciliary beating by walking along the adjacent doublet.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What do radial spokes and nexin links do in the axoneme?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Radial spokes connect the doublets to the central sheath; nexin (dynein-regulatory) links tie adjacent doublets together so that dynein-driven sliding is converted into bending.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What is the basal body and how does its structure differ from the axoneme?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: The basal body anchors the cilium and is a centriole-derived structure of nine microtubule triplets (9x3) with no central pair, whereas the axoneme is nine doublets plus a central pair (9x2 + 2).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: How many cilia are on a ciliated cell and how long are they?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Roughly 200-300 cilia per cell, each about 5-10 micrometres long.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What is a primary cilium and why does it matter clinically?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: A single, non-motile 9+0 cilium (no central pair, no dynein arms) present on most cells as a sensory antenna; renal tubular primary cilia sense flow via polycystin-1/2, and their defects cause autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease (PKD). Primary cilia also transduce Hedgehog signalling — cilium disorders are collectively 'ciliopathies'.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Describe the two phases of the ciliary beat.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: A fast, stiff power stroke in which the tip engages the gel layer to push mucus forward, followed by a slow, curled recovery stroke within the watery sol layer.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What is a metachronal wave and how fast does it move mucus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Neighbouring cilia beating slightly out of phase produce a coordinated wave that propels mucus at about 1 cm/min toward the pharynx (beat frequency ~12-15 Hz).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Why is periciliary (sol) layer depth critical for clearance?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Cilia must beat within a watery sol layer of the right depth; if the mucus is dehydrated (as in CF) the layer collapses and clearance stalls even though the cilia are structurally normal.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Contrast the cores and motility of cilia, microvilli and stereocilia.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Cilia have a microtubule (9+2) core and are motile (dynein-powered); microvilli and stereocilia have actin cores and are non-motile (stereocilia are giant microvilli, not true cilia).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What is primary ciliary dyskinesia?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: An autosomal recessive disorder of ciliary structure — most often an outer/inner dynein-arm defect (DNAH5), but also radial-spoke, central-pair or nexin-DRC defects — causing dyskinetic (or immotile) cilia and failed mucociliary clearance; screened by low nasal nitric oxide and confirmed with high-speed video microscopy, EM and genetics.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: List the features of Kartagener syndrome.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: A subset of primary ciliary dyskinesia comprising situs inversus, bronchiectasis and chronic sinusitis, often with infertility and recurrent otitis media.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Why does primary ciliary dyskinesia cause situs inversus in ~50% of patients?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Embryonic nodal cilia are unusual — 9+0 (no central pair) but still MOTILE, rotating to generate leftward nodal flow that sets left-right asymmetry; when they are immotile, laterality is randomised, so about half of PCD patients develop situs inversus.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: How does cystic fibrosis impair mucociliary clearance if the cilia are normal?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: A CFTR defect produces dehydrated, abnormally thick and sticky mucus; the cilia are structurally normal but cannot move the viscous mucus, so the escalator jams and infection/bronchiectasis follow.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: State the key contrast between PCD and CF.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Both cause bronchiectasis and sinusitis, but PCD is a ciliary (motor) defect whereas CF is a mucus (hydration/CFTR) defect with structurally normal cilia.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What is goblet-cell hyperplasia and what causes it?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: An increase in goblet-cell number (or their appearance in normally goblet-free sites, i.e. metaplasia) from chronic irritation such as smoking, asthma or chronic bronchitis, causing mucus hypersecretion.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: How does smoking affect the mucociliary apparatus?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: Smoke paralyses and strips cilia and drives squamous metaplasia while increasing goblet cells/mucus, so clearance falls and secretions accumulate (smoker's cough).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: Why does primary ciliary dyskinesia often cause male infertility?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: The sperm flagellum shares the same 9+2 axoneme and dynein motors, so the same defect renders sperm immotile.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: How is cystic fibrosis diagnosed, and why are affected men usually infertile?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: By a raised sweat chloride (>60 mmol/L) — CFTR normally reabsorbs Cl- in sweat ducts, so its loss gives salty sweat; the commonest mutation is ΔF508 (autosomal recessive). Male infertility is due to congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD) — obstructive, with normal spermatogenesis, unlike the immotile-sperm infertility of PCD.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.front: What is the ciliary rootlet?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & C.back: A striated cytoskeletal structure extending from the basal body into the cytoplasm that anchors the cilium.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What does 'lung parenchyma' mean?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: The functional gas-exchange tissue of the lung — respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli — held in an elastic connective-tissue framework.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Distinguish the conducting from the respiratory portion of the lung.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Conducting portion (no gas exchange): trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles. Respiratory portion (gas exchange = parenchyma): respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, alveoli.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What is a bronchovascular bundle?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: An airway travelling together with an accompanying branch of the pulmonary artery of similar calibre; finding one locates the other.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Where do pulmonary veins run, relative to the airways?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Separately from the airways, out in the interlobular septa (not within the bronchovascular bundle).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Define the pulmonary acinus.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Everything distal to a single terminal bronchiole (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, sacs and alveoli) — the functional gas-exchange unit.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Define the pulmonary lobule.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: The secondary pulmonary lobule — the smallest lung unit bounded by connective-tissue interlobular septa, supplied by several (~3-5) terminal bronchioles and containing multiple acini; it is the unit of HRCT interpretation. (The tissue distal to ONE terminal bronchiole is the acinus.)

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Define a bronchopulmonary segment and its clinical relevance.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: A region supplied by a segmental bronchus with its own segmental artery; it is a surgically resectable unit (segmentectomy).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What epithelium forms the pleura?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Simple squamous mesothelium over a thin layer of elastic connective tissue.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Distinguish visceral and parietal pleura, including innervation.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Visceral pleura covers the lung (autonomic innervation, insensate to pain; bronchial/pulmonary blood supply); parietal pleura lines the chest wall (somatic innervation via intercostal/phrenic nerves, pain-sensitive; systemic blood supply).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Which pleura is responsible for pleuritic pain, and why?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: The parietal pleura, because it has somatic (intercostal/phrenic) innervation; the visceral pleura is insensate.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What is in the pleural cavity normally?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: A thin film of serous fluid that lubricates movement of the two pleural layers against each other.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Describe the two components of the lung's dual blood supply.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: The pulmonary circulation carries deoxygenated blood for gas exchange (low pressure, high flow, follows the airways); the bronchial circulation carries systemic oxygenated blood that nourishes the airways, vessels and pleura.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Why do pulmonary emboli rarely cause lung infarction?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Because the lung has a dual blood supply (pulmonary and bronchial); if pulmonary flow is blocked, the bronchial circulation usually keeps the tissue alive unless it too is compromised (e.g. in heart failure).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Contrast the central and peripheral bronchogenic carcinomas.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Central (hilar, smoking-related): squamous cell carcinoma (keratin pearls) and small-cell carcinoma (neuroendocrine, paraneoplastic). Peripheral: adenocarcinoma (commonest, TTF-1/Napsin A positive, glands/mucin, also in non-smokers) and large-cell carcinoma.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What does the lung's elastic-fibre framework do?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: It provides elastic recoil for expiration and holds the bronchioles open by radial traction; it extends from the pleura through the septa around airways and vessels.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What does the pulmonary interstitium contain?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: The connective tissue of the septa — collagen and elastin plus fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells and occasional lymphocytes; it has a thin (exchange) side and a thick (support) side.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Describe the lymphatic drainage of the lung.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Two plexuses — a superficial (pleural) and a deep (bronchovascular) network — draining to the hilar lymph nodes; notably, there are no lymphatics in the alveolar walls themselves.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What is BALT?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue — mucosal lymphoid aggregates guarding the airways.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Name the two opposite ways the connective-tissue framework can fail.
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Loss of elastin causes emphysema (floppy, over-inflated, obstructive); expansion of the interstitium with collagen causes fibrosis (stiff, restricted).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Which stain demonstrates the lung's elastic framework and is useful in emphysema and pleural invasion?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Elastic stains such as Verhoeff-van Gieson or orcein.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Which stain highlights interstitial fibrosis?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Masson trichrome (collagen stains blue/green).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: Which immunomarkers identify mesothelial cells (e.g. mesothelioma)?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Calretinin and WT-1.

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What is emphysema at the tissue level and its two main patterns?
histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.back: Destruction of elastin and alveolar walls causing permanent airspace enlargement and loss of recoil; centriacinar (smoking-related, upper zones) and panacinar (alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, lower zones).

histology__RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma.front: What is the histological hallmark of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
